title: 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5: Here's what we still like, here's what annoys us
gist: Five years after launch, the Hyundai Ioniq 5 still holds up on fast-charging and styling, but the 2026 AWD Limited trades range for power, has an annoying touch-sensitive climate panel, and carries a known Integrated Charging Controller Unit (ICCU) failure risk that Hyundai has addressed with a 15-year/180,000-mile warranty extension rather than a full fix.

insights.claim: The 2026 Ioniq 5 lineup starts at $35,000 for the standard-range model, while the range-topping AWD Limited trim tested starts at $45,075, with AWD itself adding $3,900 over the rear-wheel-drive version.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A roughly $10,000 spread between base and top trim, with AWD alone costing $3,900, frames the Ioniq 5's real-world competitive pricing band against rival compact EV crossovers.

insights.claim: The reviewer says he would personally choose the rear-wheel-drive Ioniq 5 for its extra range and would not pay up for the Limited trim over the $39,800 SEL, since most desirable features are standard on the SEL.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: An expert reviewer's value pick (SEL over Limited, RWD over AWD) signals where real demand and resale value may concentrate in this segment, useful for parts/aftermarket and trim-mix demand forecasting.
insights.locator: But were I buying my own Ioniq 5

insights.claim: The off-road-oriented XRT trim costs $46,275 and sacrifices about 10 miles (16 km) of range compared to the AWD Limited, a tradeoff likely to deter more rational buyers from choosing it.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Niche off-road EV trims carry a clear range penalty, a factor relevant to how automakers price and market rugged EV variants against mainstream buyer priorities.
insights.locator: This is the most expensive Ioniq 5 variant

insights.claim: The AWD Ioniq 5 Limited has an EPA range of 269 miles versus 318 miles for the rear-wheel-drive variant, illustrating the roughly 15% range penalty from adding a second drive motor.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A clear, quantified AWD range tax is a data point buyers and fleet planners can use when weighing traction benefits against usable range in EV crossovers.
insights.locator: The AWD version has an EPA range of 269 miles

insights.claim: Single-motor Ioniq 5s can achieve roughly 4 miles/kWh (15.5 kWh/100 km) efficiency, while the AWD version manages closer to 3.4 miles/kWh (18.3 kWh/100 km) even in Eco mode.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A roughly 15% efficiency gap between single- and dual-motor configurations quantifies the real operating-cost tradeoff of AWD for EV owners and fleet TCO models.
insights.locator: Single-motor Ioniq 5s should easily be capable

insights.claim: The Ioniq 5's native NACS (J3400) port, added in the 2025 refresh, lets it charge at Tesla Superchargers as well as IONNA and Electrify America, but most Tesla Superchargers are older V3 units capped at 250 kW with shorter cables that are awkward for non-Tesla EVs, resulting in longer charge times than 350 kW or 400 kW chargers.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Native NACS adoption expands charger access for non-Tesla EVs, but the installed base of older, power-capped V3 Superchargers means the charging-speed benefit of NACS access is currently overstated for 800V vehicles like the Ioniq 5.
insights.locator: In practice, the ubiquity of Tesla’s charging locations

insights.claim: A 240V Level 2 AC home charger takes about 7 hours 20 minutes to charge the Ioniq 5 from 10-100%, positioning home charging as the practical default for most owners rather than frequent DC fast-charging.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Reinforces that home Level 2 charging, not costly DC fast-charging networks, should be the primary use case investors and infrastructure planners size for mainstream EV ownership.
insights.locator: A 240 V level 2 AC charger should take

insights.claim: The Ioniq 5's Integrated Charging Controller Unit (ICCU), which charges the 12V accessory battery from the 800V traction battery, can fail if its MOSFET is subjected to overvoltage at the start/end of charging or overheats during charging or driving, in some cases stranding the car on the highway.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A specific hardware failure mechanism causing highway breakdowns is a material safety and reliability liability for Hyundai's E-GMP platform vehicles, relevant to warranty cost exposure and brand risk.
insights.locator: the Ioniq 5’s biggest problem is the potential specter

insights.claim: Hyundai's December 2024 recall estimated only about 1% of vehicles were affected by the ICCU issue, but Consumer Reports survey data shows the actual incidence across E-GMP platform EVs (including the Ioniq 5) is between 2-10%.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A gap between the automaker's official 1% failure estimate and independent survey data showing 2-10% suggests Hyundai may be materially understating the ICCU defect rate, a warranty-liability and reputational risk to model against reserve estimates.
insights.locator: Hyundai issued a recall in December 2024

insights.claim: Rather than a fix, Hyundai USA responded to the ICCU problem by extending the component's warranty to 15 years or 180,000 miles, effectively covering the defect for most of a vehicle's lifespan instead of resolving the underlying hardware issue.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Extending warranty coverage rather than issuing a hardware fix defers cost recognition and signals Hyundai may be managing a known, unresolved defect rate rather than eliminating it — a potential future recall or liability overhang.
insights.locator: Hyundai USA recently increased the warranty on the ICCU

insights.claim: The reviewer dislikes the Ioniq 5's touch-sensitive climate control panel, citing weak backlighting that's hard to see in bright sunlight, difficulty building muscle memory versus physical buttons, and visible dust accumulation on the panel.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Persistent criticism of touch-based climate controls versus physical buttons is a recurring UX complaint across the EV industry relevant to automaker interior-design decisions and consumer satisfaction scores.
insights.locator: I am definitely going on record as not liking

insights.claim: The blind-spot view monitor, which uses wing-mirror cameras to show the relevant blind spot when signaling, is highlighted as a genuinely useful feature for checking traffic in protected bike lanes.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Camera-based blind-spot monitoring is called out as a differentiated safety feature that could influence trim-level purchase decisions and safety-rating perception.
insights.locator: One of the Limited’s features that I rather like
